title: The Carp in the Mud
part: PART ONE: THE SUN GOES OUT

pages.text:
*The Gatekeeper's Rules, Rule 1: Water always finds its level, and it is never impatient about it.*

On the morning the sun went out of the east half of the lake, Shu Tsai was standing in her green rain boots in the middle of what had been a fishing cove, holding a bamboo pole upright in the mud and explaining to forty-one stranded carp that none of this was her fault.

The carp, to their credit, listened. They lay in a scatter of shallow puddles with their gold-bronze sides heaving and their round mouths opening and closing like a council of very old men who have lost the thread of the argument. Behind them the lake, which had stood against the cove's stone steps at bedtime the night before, had drawn back a full hundred meters in the dark, as neatly as a tablecloth being pulled off a table, and left everything on it standing. There were upturned dinghies. There was a rope that had once held a boat. There was a single blue flip-flop, set at an angle that suggested it was still waiting for its owner to come back and finish the thought.

It was barely six. The mist was lifting off Two-Light Lake in long slow sheets, and under it the camphor ridges stood up out of the whiteness like folded green paper, and somewhere in the bamboo above the terraces a blue magpie was complaining in a voice like a rusty hinge. Shu was sixteen. She had slept four hours, her braid was coming loose from its red cord, and she was in possession of exactly one fact, which she meant to protect: whatever had happened to the lake, it had happened to the *east* half only.

"What do carp eat," asked a small voice behind her, "when there isn't a lake?"
pages.image: Early morning in a drained fishing cove on a misty highland lake: Shu, a sixteen-year-old girl with light warm-ivory skin, one long thick black braid with a red cord, a dark-indigo cotton jacket and green rubber rain boots, stands in grey mud holding a bamboo pole upright, with small puddles of stranded golden carp around her, green camphor ridges rising out of white mist, and a stone stair leading down to a lake that has pulled back far away.

pages.text:
Tsai Bao, who was eleven and went by A-Bao to everyone including his teachers, stood at the edge of the stone steps in a yellow raincoat that came down to his sandals, holding a bamboo basket in both arms as though it contained the crown jewels. It contained a duckling. The duckling was named Dumpling and had been awake for exactly as long as A-Bao had, which was too long, and it was peering over the rim of the basket at the mud with the expression of a creature who has been promised a swimming lesson and is beginning to suspect fraud.

"They eat what they always eat," said Shu. "Mud and small things. But they need the water to carry the small things to them. It is the water that does the feeding. The carp only open their mouths."

"So the lake was the table," said A-Bao.

"Yes."

"And now there's no table."

"There is a table," said Shu. "It has moved. Hold the pole."

She took out of her collar the thing she carried everywhere, a brass plumb bob the size of a plum on a long cord, its bamboo handle worn smooth by her grandfather's hand and then her own, and hung it from the top of the pole. It swung once, steadied and hung perfectly still: the one object in the world, her grandfather liked to say, that never told a lie about *down*. Beside the cove's stone steps the old keepers had cut a line into the rock with a chisel, a notch the width of a thumb, and beside the notch a character so weathered that only the family could read it. *Level.* The notch was where the lake belonged. Shu knelt in the mud, set her folding rule against the stone, and read the distance from the notch to the place where the water now began, a long grey way across the cove. She read it twice and a third time. Then she read it a fourth time, because the number kept being absurd.

"Two meters and ten centimeters," she said. "Below the mark."

"Is that a lot?"

"It is a lot for a lake to lose in one night, when nobody has opened a gate."

She wrote it in her notebook and underlined it twice. A-Bao looked at the underlining, then at his sister, and said with great seriousness that he would take notes on the notes.
pages.image: Shu kneels in the grey mud of the drained cove beside a stone step with an old chiseled notch, measuring with a folding rule, her brass plumb bob hanging from a bamboo pole beside her, while A-Bao, a small eleven-year-old boy with fair skin, a black bowl-cut, a bright yellow raincoat and red sandals, stands on the steps holding a bamboo basket with a small yellow duckling.

pages.text:
By seven the news had gone round Mistwater Landing the way news does in a village built on a hill above a lake, which is to say downhill, quickly and with additions. Fishermen in rubber boots came picking across the mud with nets and buckets. A woman who sold tea carried a kettle out of pure reflex and then stood in the cove holding it, unable to think what to boil it for. Aunt Meng arrived from the dock stall with a red apron over her nightclothes and a great flat net over one shoulder, a round and cheerful woman with a hair net and a voice that could hold a conversation across two ferry piers.

"The weather!" she announced to nobody and everybody. "It's the weather. It is always the weather. Last night the lake was a lake and this morning she is a puddle, and I, who have sold fish ball soup on that pier for twenty-six years, say the weather has done it. Pass me that carp. No, the other one, the sulking one."

They carried the fish in buckets across the mud to the deep channel that still held water, a procession of wet and muttering people, passing the buckets from hand to hand while the sun climbed over the ridge. The carp went in with a slap and a flash and were gone. Somebody started a rumor; it was a good rumor, because it was short and frightening. The lake, it said, had swallowed the sun. It was the old story, the dragons, the two lights, and the east half of the lake, the half that was shaped like the sun, was dark now, wasn't it, and dry, and gone.

"That's not what happened," said Shu, to a fisherman who was standing very close to her with a bucket and a look of reverent dread.

"No?" said the fisherman. "Then what happened?"

She opened her mouth and, to her great annoyance, found that she did not know.
pages.image: A crowd of villagers in rubber boots crossing the wide grey mud of the drained cove passing buckets of golden carp toward a narrow deep channel, among them Aunt Meng, a round smiling fifty-year-old woman with warm tan skin, hair in a net and a red apron, holding a big net, with Shu and A-Bao in the foreground and misty green ridges behind.

pages.text:
She did know one other thing. It had occurred to her somewhere between the third bucket and the fourth, and it sat in the back of her mind like a stone in a shoe. When she was small, her grandfather had taken her out in the Magpie, the village ferry, and shown her the lake from the middle: two bays of water curving away on either side of Lantern Island, the east one round and wide, the west one a thin silver crescent, so that from the ridge above the whole thing looked exactly like the old coin of sun and moon on the temple door. East was the Sun Basin. West was the Moon Basin. Between them the island with its red lanterns, and under the island, somewhere, the channel where the two halves of the lake touched.

She turned and looked west across the island. Then she stopped holding the bucket.

The Moon Basin was *high*. Even from here, across the island's green back and the red lantern roofs of the temple, she could see how the dark water lay up against its far bank like a full cup that a nervous waiter is carrying across a room. It lapped at the foot of the Lantern Temple's lowest steps. It crowded the stone wall below the lower village. One half of the lake was empty, and the other was very nearly full, and a person with any common sense and a ruler would have wanted to know whether those two facts belonged together.

"A-gong," said A-Bao, and pointed.

Her grandfather had come down to the water's edge, a slight lame figure in a faded grey padded vest and a straw hat, leaning on his bamboo cane, and for some time he stood quite still and looked at the mud as though it had insulted him. He did not look at the carp. He did not look at the people. He looked at the long, bare, shining floor of the cove where the lake had been, and Shu, watching his face, saw something cross it that she would later have trouble describing. It was not surprise. Nobody could have called it surprise.

"Go home," said A-gong, in his dry gentle voice, "and eat."
pages.image: At the edge of the drained cove, A-gong, a lame seventy-four-year-old grandfather with pale tan skin, thin white hair and a short white beard, a faded grey padded vest, a straw hat and a bamboo cane, stands very still looking at the mud, while in the distance across a green island with red-lantern temple roofs a dark full crescent-shaped lake presses against a stone wall; Shu and A-Bao stand beside him.

pages.text:
At home, in the courtyard behind the house with the tin roof, the tea leaves were drying on their bamboo trays in the new sun, and A-gong sat in his cane chair beside them with his hat on his knee and would not explain anything at all.

Shu tried. She tried with rice porridge and with pickled radish, with a question about the notch in the stone and another about the old lake, in her most reasonable voice and then in her most pitiable one. Her grandfather ate his porridge. He wiped his bowl with a piece of bread. He said, once, that the tea would be ready by the end of the week if the rain held off, and the whole sentence was like a door shutting very softly at the far end of a long corridor. A-Bao, who understood the grammar of silence rather better than most eleven-year-olds, went to teach Dumpling to float in the washtub.

She sat down on the doorstep with her notebook. *2.1 m*, it said, in her own square handwriting, and she underlined it a third time. Under it she wrote, because she had been taught to write down what she did not know as carefully as what she did: *West basin high. East basin low. Why both?* And under that, more slowly: *Who closed the lake?*

The sun moved across the trays. Behind her grandfather's chair, hanging from a nail in the wall where it had hung for as long as she had been alive, was the brass key on its faded cord, the one she had never once seen him use. It looked, in the afternoon light, very much like a key that had been waiting a long time for someone to ask what it opened.

She did not ask. Not yet. But she wrote *KEY?* on the corner of the page, and drew a small, careful circle around it, and counted the days on her fingers, though she did not yet know that there were thirty of them, nor what they were for.
pages.image: In a sunlit courtyard of a house with a tin roof, trays of drying tea leaves in the afternoon light, A-gong sits in a cane chair with his straw hat on his knee, in the foreground Shu sits on the doorstep writing in a notebook, and on the wall behind the chair hangs a brass key on a faded cord.
